messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 32
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Park Ranger
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 41

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction, Emotional Numbing: I numb my feelings, Avoid Driving: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle
  Threat: Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening, Door and Lock Checking: I repeatedly check that doors and windows are locked, Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
  Memory: Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank, Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
  Negative Appraisals: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened, Can't Rely on Others: I can't rely on other people, Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy

Vignette:
Ethan had been a park ranger for nearly a decade, a life he chose for its quiet solitude and the rugged self-reliance it demanded. Now, that same solitude felt like a cage. The trouble began eight months ago, during a solo backpacking trip in South America. What was meant to be a two-week trek turned into a four-day nightmare when he was abducted by a local militia. The memory of it doesn’t exist as a story in his mind. When he tries to explain what happened, perhaps to a doctor or a concerned colleague, the words catch in his throat. He loses the thread, stammering as his mind serves up a collage of sensory shrapnel instead of a sequence of events. There are moments of excruciating clarity: the abrasive scrape of a zip tie against his wrist, the overwhelming smell of gasoline and stale sweat in the back of the van, the low rumble of the engine vibrating through the floorboards. But these flashes are surrounded by complete blanks, black voids where time and action should be. He can’t seem to put the core of the frightening event into words; it lives in his body, not his vocabulary.

This bodily memory is a constant companion in his work. A tourist’s car backfiring near a trailhead sent him diving behind his patrol truck before he even registered the sound. His body had reacted to the danger before his mind had time to think, leaving him crouched and trembling, convinced that his reactions since the event mean he is going crazy. He lives with a persistent, dull ache in his right shoulder, a relic of his captivity. He has come to believe his body has been permanently damaged by what happened, a fragile thing that can no longer be trusted to protect him. This sense of physical vulnerability has bled into a profound distrust of everything else. He is certain he can’t rely on other people; after all, no one could help him then, so why would they be able to now? This conviction plays out in small, exhausting ways. Before approaching a family to warn them about a bear sighting, he must rehearse what to say over and over in his head, scripting the interaction to minimize any chance of unpredictability.

His small, isolated ranger cabin has become both a sanctuary and a prison. Each night, he performs a rigid ritual of checking and re-checking the locks on the door and the latches on the two small windows, a routine that can take up to half an hour. The fear is palpable. He has also developed an intense hypervigilance around time. When something takes longer than expected—a reply to an email from his supervisor, a scheduled supply drop that is ten minutes late—he doesn’t feel impatience, but a rising tide of panic. He assumes something terrible is happening, a catastrophe unfolding just out of sight. To manage this constant state of activation, he has found a way to simply turn it all off. The sweeping vistas from the fire tower, which once filled him with a quiet awe, now register as little more than a postcard. He stands there, waiting to feel something—anything—but the connection is gone. He knows he is numbing his feelings, a desperate attempt to mute the terror that hums just beneath the surface.

The most debilitating change has been his relationship with vehicles. Being in the back of that van, powerless and blindfolded, has poisoned the act of driving. He now avoids driving his patrol truck whenever possible, taking long, inefficient routes on foot and citing engine trouble he knows isn't real. Being a passenger is out of the question. This avoidance has started to have concrete consequences; his supervisor recently noted his failure to patrol the park's more remote northern roads. The conversation was brief, but it has left Ethan terrified of losing the one part of his old life he has left. It was this fear, the realization that his world was shrinking to the size of his cabin, that finally pushed him to seek help. He feels broken and lost, hoping for a way to quiet the alarms constantly ringing in his head, but deeply afraid that he is too far gone to ever find his way back.
